Double dose of osimertinib (160mg QD) combined with pemetrexed and platinum improves the PFS from 13.8 months to 24.9 months compared to monotherapy (Bortolot et al. ). Osimertinib combined with docetaxel (DTX) and ramucirumab (RAM) can be an alternative option, also prolonging the LM control (Tomizawa et al. ). The therapeutic effects may also be improved by combining osimertinib with capmatinib or with RT (van der Wel et al. ). Double dose of osimertinib (160mg QD) can also be combined with intrathecal pemetrexed (ITP), to enhance the control of LM (Zhong et al. ). Combination of 50mg of ITP and TKI has shown increase in the median OS (mOS) to 12 months (Fan et al. ). Bispecific drug like amivantamab or other third generation of EGFR-TKIs like lazertinib or chemotherapy can be a choice to treat drug resistance, but all need more clinical trials (van der Wel et al. ). When it comes to furmonertinib, 240 mg QD monotherapy or 160 mg QD with ITP both indicate positive results (Chen et al. , ; Yu et al. ). It lasts for a long time in the brain tissue. Single agent of 160 mg furmonertinib or in combination of anti-angiogenic agent is recommended after failure of the prior EGFR-TKI treatment (Xu et al. ). Aumolertinib (110 mg QD, not high dose), provides irreversible inhibition (Qin et al. ; Zhuang et al. ), and increases the intracranial Disease Control Rate (DCR) to 91.3%. Consequently, combined utilization of aumolertinib and furmonertinib is highly selective in surrounding the metabolites center of tumor in the brain and can have double effects in inhibiting tumor growth, based on the clinical use (Jia et al. ). Meanwhile, zorifertinib performs well in CNS penetration and has promising effects together with lazertinib and amivantamab (Bian et al. ). Afatinib, belonging to the second generation of EGFR-TKIs can deal with the drug resistance of the first and third generation like icotinib and osimertinib, also used to treat compound mutations (Li et al. ).The fourth generation of EGFR-TKIs including BLU-945 has not shown efficacy to date in trials (Wu et al. , ). Regimens centered on radiotherapy Radiotherapy (RT) is another treatment option besides chemotherapy or targeted therapy (Morris et al. ). Radiotherapy, including WBRT or focal spine RT, provides faster symptom relief, such as reducing intracranial pressure or alleviating spinal cord compression, making it more suitable for urgent, symptomatic cases (Buszek and Chung ). Furthermore, RT is better for managing bulky or focal disease, as it can directly target and shrink visible lesions. Recent studies have shown that proton craniospinal irradiation (pCSI) performed better in improving CNS progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) for patients with NSCLC with LM with no increase in serious treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) (Yang et al. ). WBRT is a branch method of RT. The outcomes after treatment with WBRT remains poor, without improvement in QOL (Oyoshi et al. ). LM patients with EGFR mutations are likely to gain limited benefits from WBRT, except in cases of typical and serious CNS symptoms (Zhen et al. ), to assist in prolonging OS for patients. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is frequently combined with WBRT for treatment. However, when radiation therapy (RT) is used alone, it often leads to a poorer outcomes (Economopoulou and Mountzios ; Wong et al. ). According to QUARTZ trial, no clear survival advantage or improvement in quality of life was shown for patients that were treated with RT. Multivariate analysis has shown that, in patients with LM who have undergone SRS, chemotherapy and targeted therapy post-SRS are associated with improved survival (Chiang et al. ). Radiotherapy has several limitations in treating LM in NSCLC, including short-term efficacy, toxicity, inability to treat diffuse disease, and limited impact on overall survival. While it can provide palliative benefits, its role is often constrained by the diffuse nature of LM and the poor tolerance of patients with advanced disease. Combining radiotherapy with systemic therapies like targeted therapies and immunotherapy and exploring novel techniques including proton or intrathecal therapies has been proven to help overcome some of these limitations. Regimens centered on anti-angiogenic drugs For patients with EGFR-sensitive mutations, the combination of EGFR-TKIs and anti-angiogenic drugs is an exploratory treatment strategy, and more clinical trials are still needed (Yi et al. ). Bevacizumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that targets vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), inhibiting its biological activity and suppressing angiogenesis. By blocking VEGF, it normalizes tumor vasculature, reducing tumor growth and enhancing the delivery of other therapies, making it a key anti-angiogenic treatment for various cancers (Garcia et al. ). Osimertinib (Third-Generation EGFR-TKI) combined with Bevacizumab (Anti-VEGF Monoclonal Antibody) is a well recommended option

these limitations. Bevacizumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that targets vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), inhibiting its biological activity and suppressing angiogenesis. By blocking VEGF, it normalizes tumor vasculature, reducing tumor growth and enhancing the delivery of other therapies, making it a key anti-angiogenic treatment for various cancers (Garcia et al. ). Osimertinib (Third-Generation EGFR-TKI) combined with Bevacizumab (Anti-VEGF Monoclonal Antibody) is a well recommended option (Lu et al. ). Just as mentioned above, osimertinib has strong BBB penetration and significant efficacy against LM, meanwhile bevacizumab may enhance efficacy by inhibiting angiogenesis and reducing cerebral edema. Bevacizumab with RT is a recommended pair in improving control of CNS metastasis with high sensitivity, helping to normalize the tumor affected blood cells (Wu et al. , ). The efficacy and safety of osimertinib plus bevacizumab in the treatment of advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients are more obvious in terms of short-term efficacy compared with the long-term effects (Leong et al. ). The objective response rate (ORR) of the experimental group was significantly higher than that of the control group, and the disease control rate (DCR) was slightly higher than the control group. Studies have indicated that a combination therapy consisting of the standard oral dose of osimertinib (80 mg QD) and a moderate dose of bevacizumab (7.5 mg/kg q3w) may represent the optimal treatment regimen for patients with advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC (Yao et al. ). Furmonertinib 160 mg with or without bevacizuamb or anlotinib represents a promising treatment option for patients with advanced NSCLC who experience resistance following third-generation EGFR-TKI therapy, particularly in cases where resistance is driven by the progression of intracranial lesions (Xu et al. ). It demonstrates notable efficacy and a manageable safety profile, making it a compelling candidate for further investigation. Regimens centered on intrathecal chemotherapy For patients with LM, intrathecal chemotherapy is an effective treatment option. Administration methods include conventional lumbar puncture and delivery via an Ommaya reservoir. Compared to lumbar puncture, Ommaya reservoir administration offers the advantage of direct drug delivery into the most proximal point of CSF circulation. This ensures uniform distribution throughout the ventricular system, thereby enhancing local drug concentration (Sandberg et al. ). However, no established consensus currently exists regarding optimal therapeutic protocols, including drug selection, dosing regimens, or treatment cycles, for either intrathecal or intraventricular chemotherapy via Ommaya reservoir. LM has been typically managed through the direct intrathecal administration of chemotherapeutic agents, such as methotrexate, cytarabine (including its liposomal formulation), and thiotepa till now, often combined with systemic platinum (Wu et al. ; Chen et al. , ). Pemetrexed, a multi-target antifolate drug, has limited BBB penetration; however, in LM, increased BBB permeability may enable therapeutic concentrations in the CSF. Methotrexate is another intrathecal treatment option for LM. There is limited data directly comparing the efficacy of intrathecal methotrexate with that of pemetrexed, but it still can be combined with systematic chemotherapy as an option when drug resistance is developed (Gwak et al. ; Zhou et al. ). In most patients (9 out of 10) receiving intrathecal pemetrexed at doses of 20 mg or 25 mg, LM-related clinical manifestations showed improvement. The enhanced efficacy observed may be associated with the higher dose of pemetrexed. Furthermore, among the 14 EGFR-mutated patients who switched to alternative antitumor agents, 12 of which experienced improvement in LM-related symptoms following a combination of intrathecal pemetrexed and tailored systemic therapies. These results suggest that intrathecal pemetrexed, particularly at higher doses and in combination with systemic treatments, may be an effective approach for managing LM in NSCLC patients (Fan et al. ). Currently, there is no standardized treatment protocol; further research is necessary. Future options: regimens centered on immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) ICIs have long been applied in the treatment of NSCLC, but it remains controversial in LM because few improvements have been witnessed. The reason why ICIs show limitation is that targeting at T cells, whose concentration is lower in CSF, it cannot fulfill its intended functions. Consequently, increasing the concentration of T cells in the major task in the combined therapy before using ICIs. A retrospective study reported that among 37 NSCLC-LM patients with targetable mutations who received ICI treatment, the median PFS was 2.5 months and the median OS was 5.8 months (Stang ). This suggests that some patients with targetable genomic alterations may derive benefit from ICI therapy following LM diagnosis. Recent studies have indicated that combining radiation therapy with immunotherapy can enhance both local and distant cancer control. This is achieved by stimulating the immune response, ultimately leading to improved survival rates. It seems that radiation therapy strengthens the immune system

A retrospective study reported that among 37 NSCLC-LM patients with targetable mutations who received ICI treatment, the median PFS was 2.5 months and the median OS was 5.8 months (Stang ). This suggests that some patients with targetable genomic alterations may derive benefit from ICI therapy following LM diagnosis. Recent studies have indicated that combining radiation therapy with immunotherapy can enhance both local and distant cancer control. This is achieved by stimulating the immune response, ultimately leading to improved survival rates. It seems that radiation therapy strengthens the immune system by activating T cells, dendritic cells, and other immune cells within the tumor microenvironment (Tagliaferri et al. ). This process also involves releasing tumor-associated antigens and optimizing antigen presentation (Ji et al. ). Furthermore, radiation therapy targeting the brain may temporarily disrupt the BBB, allowing more peripheral effector T cells to enter the CSF. If necessary, PD1/PD-L1 drugs can be beneficial in treating drug resistance. Furthermore, cytotoxic chemotherapy and molecular targeted therapies other than ICIs improve survival (Nakagawa et al. ), which is another alternative after drug resistance. As for ICIs, local delivery of dual-stem cells expressing oncolytic herpes simplex virus (oHSV) and a single-chain variable fragment of programmed death-1 antibody (scFvPD-1) effectively targets and modulates the immunosuppressive TME in the context of lung-to-leptomeningeal metastasis. Engineered allogeneic stem cells orchestrate T lymphocyte presents a promising therapeutic strategy for the management of LM (Kanaya et al. ). Studies of relevant genes of LM of EGFR mutated NSCLC provides new methods and innovations for treatment. CDKN2A aberration is closely connected wo adverse LM prognosis therefore the interaction between CDK4/6 inhibitors and EGFR-TKIs is worth investigating (Miao et al. ; Zheng et al. ). The drug resistance has been proven to be connected with the interactions between CD47 and SIRPA. Consequently, destruction of such interactions may be a new type of therapy (Li et al. ). The process of tumor cells entering the brain and meninges including detachment, invasion, transmission and crossing of BBB and brain clone growth can be new targets with the CSF and Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) related tests (Liu et al. ). Discussion LM is a devastating complication in patients with advanced cancer, carrying a poor prognosis. Its incidence is rising with advancements in systemic cancer therapies. Clinical management remains challenging due to limited therapeutic options, further constrained by inadequate blood–brain barrier penetration, acquired drug resistance, and uncertainty regarding optimal treatment sequencing. Research efforts should focus not only on developing next-generation EGFR-TKIs but also on exploring molecular-level therapeutic strategies to combat LM. Additionally, therapeutic approaches may include systemic chemotherapy, immunotherapy, combination therapies, and local intrathecal chemotherapy. As current evidence primarily stems from isolated studies and case reports, rigorous randomized controlled trials are essential to fully elucidate the role of EGFR-TKIs in LM management. Such trials will facilitate the selection of more effective treatments and optimize therapeutic approaches.

In 2021, the World Health Organization updated the classification of Central Nervous System (CNS) tumors to restrict glioblastomas to isocitrate dehydrogenase-wildtype (IDHwt) tumors, improving understanding of the prognosis and optimal therapy for these tumors. This revision also enables more homogeneous populations of patients to be enrolled in clinical trials, facilitating the evaluation of novel therapies. In this updated consensus review from the Society for Neuro-Oncology (SNO) and the European Association of Neuro-Oncology (EANO), the current management of patients with glioblastoma is discussed. In addition, novel therapies such as immunotherapies, viral therapies, targeted molecular therapies, theranostics, and antibody–drug conjugates will be reviewed, as well as the current challenges and future directions for research.
